## What you will and will not learn today

```{webr-r}
#| context: setup
# Every object a slide uses, created when the page loads, so each code area
# runs on its own and in any order.
yields <- c(150, 162, NA, 171)
a <- 1
b <- "R rocks"
d <- 1 == 2
average_yield <- mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)
v <- c(4, 3, 5, 9, 1)
mixed <- c(4, 3, "5", 9, 1)
yield_data <- data.frame(
  nitrogen = c(200, 180, 300),
  yield = c(240, 220, 230),
  state = c("Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa")
)
a_list <- list(numbers = c(10, 20), state = "Iowa", data = yield_data)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The plan

An AI assistant can write R code. What it cannot do is tell you whether that code did what you needed. To judge that, you have to be able to **read** R code: say what each line does, even if you could not have written it yourself.

This course works in R. AI agents also write a lot of **Python**, the other language most used for data work, so this lecture shows each idea in both. The ideas are the same in the two languages; only the way they are written differs.

This first lecture gives you the foundation for reading code. Every line of R or Python you will see is built from three things:

1. **Objects**: named things that hold values, created with `<-` in R and `=` in Python
2. **Functions**: commands that take inputs and give back a result
3. **Packages**: collections of functions written by other people, which you install and then load

You will not learn to write these from memory. You will learn to recognise them, so that when an AI hands you code, you can follow it line by line.

### Directions

+ To study this deck you need only this web page. Every example runs inside the slides (next tab).
+ Have an AI assistant available: a chat assistant in your browser, or an agent such as Claude Code in your editor or terminal
+ To move around these slides: click the three stacked horizontal lines in the bottom-left corner for the table of contents, or press the `o` key to see every slide at once

### Running the examples

R and Python both run inside this web page, so you can run every example on these slides yourself. The first time the page opens, they take a little while to load; a code area works once its button reads "Run Code".

+ The box with the pale blue background is a **code area**. You can edit the code in it.
+ Click **Run Code** to run all the code in the code area. The result appears under it, or beside it.
+ To run only part of the code, select it and press **Command + Enter** (Mac) or **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows).
+ The reload button puts the original code back. The copy button copies the code.
+ The eye button hides the result, and a second click shows it again.
+ A Python code area says "Python" in its bar. Where R and Python sit side by side, R is on the left.

The R objects the slides use, such as `yields`, are created when the page loads, and each Python code area creates what it uses, so every code area runs on its own, in any order. Changing a number and running the code again is the quickest way to see what a line does; nothing you type here can break anything.

:::

## Why the course works this way

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R does exactly what the code says

R runs each line exactly as written. Given a line it cannot make sense of, it stops and prints an **error**. Given a line it can run, it follows its own rules, even when the result is not what you meant.

An AI assistant is the opposite. Given a request with gaps, it fills them in with guesses: where your files are, what your data holds, what you wanted the result for. It writes code that runs, and the guesses are inside it.

So the risk has moved. Code that does not run is easy to spot. Code that runs and does the wrong thing is not, and that is what you have to catch.

### Your job, and the AI's

| The AI does | You do |
|---|---|
| Knows every function and every input | Understand the step: what it is for, and what has to be true for it to work (**the concept**) |
| Writes the code | Recognise what each line does (**reading code**) |
| Fills gaps with guesses | Tell it what it cannot know: your files, your data, your purpose (**asking**) |
| Reports that the code ran | Decide whether the result is right, using checks whose answer you know in advance (**checking**) |

Every lecture in this course is organised around those four parts.

### What the course is for

By the end, you should be able to carry out your own research in R with an AI assistant writing the code: get data in, reshape it, make figures and tables, report the results, and work with maps.

In this course the AI writes that code into a **Quarto document**, a way of working we recommend for your own research too (a `.qmd` file: plain text with R code in it). **Rendering** the document runs its code from the top and makes a web page showing the code and its results. Chapter 2 teaches Quarto.

:::

# R

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## R and Python

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The languages

**R** is a programming language for statistics and data, and the program that runs code written in it.

+ Free and open source, and widely used in universities and in industry
+ Started as software for statistics, designed by statisticians
+ Grows through its users: new statistical methods often appear first as R packages written by the people who developed the method, and R also handles maps and large datasets

**Python** is a general-purpose programming language, also free and open source. It is widely used for data work and machine learning, and for automating tasks on a computer.

### Comments and output

Anything after `#` on a line is a **comment**: R and Python both ignore it. Comments explain the code to people.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: comments
# this whole line is a comment
2 + 3 # a comment can follow code on the same line
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
# this whole line is a comment
2 + 3 # a comment can follow code on the same line
```
:::
::::

In R's output, the `[1]` at the start is not part of the result. It says the line of output starts with the first value. Python prints the value alone.

:::

# Reading code

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## The three building blocks in one line

Here is a typical line of R, of the kind an AI writes all the time:

```{webr-r}
#| label: one-line
average_yield <- mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)
```

| Piece | What it is | Slide |
|---|---|---|
| `average_yield` | The name of a new **object**, which will hold the result | Objects and `<-` |
| `<-` | Stores the result of the right-hand side under that name | Objects and `<-` |
| `mean` | A **function**: it computes an average | Functions and their inputs |
| `yields` | An existing object, the first **input** to the function | Functions and their inputs |
| `na.rm = TRUE` | A named input: an option that changes what the function does | Functions and their inputs |

The same line in Python, as an AI would write it: `average_yield = yields.mean(skipna=True)`. The pieces are the same: a new object, the sign that stores it (`=`), a function (`mean`), the object it works on (`yields`) and an option (`skipna=True`).

`mean()` is built into R. Many functions are not: they come from a **package**, which has to be installed and loaded first (slide "Packages").

The rest of this section takes the pieces one at a time. By the end of it, you should be able to read the line above out loud: "compute the average of `yields`, leaving out missing values, and store it as `average_yield`".

## Objects and `<-`, `=`

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The pattern

An **object** is a named thing the computer holds in memory: a number, some text, a table of data, a fitted model. Every object is made by the same pattern, `name <- value` in R and `name = value` in Python:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| `name` | The name you will use to refer to the object later |
| `<-` (R), `=` (Python) | "Store the right-hand side under this name". Read it as "gets": `a` gets 1 |
| `value` | Anything that produces a result: a number, text, or a whole calculation |

The right-hand side is worked out **first**, then the result is stored. So `d <- 1 == 2` stores `FALSE`, the answer to "is 1 equal to 2?", not the question.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: assign
a <- 1
b <- "R rocks"
d <- 1 == 2
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
a = 1
b = "R rocks"
d = 1 == 2
```
:::
::::

Running this prints nothing: storing an object does not show it.

### Printing an object

Printing an object shows what it holds. This is the simplest check there is: did the object get the value you expected? In R, running an object's name on its own prints it; in Python, `print()` does.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: print-object
a
b
d
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
a = 1
b = "R rocks"
d = 1 == 2
print(a)
print(b)
print(d)
```
:::
::::

Python writes the two logical values `True` and `False`; R writes `TRUE` and `FALSE`.

### Overwriting

Storing under a name that already exists **replaces** the old object, without a warning:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: overwrite
a <- 3
a <- 1
a
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
a = 3
a = 1
print(a)
```
:::
::::

### `<-` versus `=`

In R, outside a function, `name = value` does the same as `name <- value`. You will see both in AI-written R code; this course uses `<-`. Python has only `=`.

Inside a function's parentheses, `=` means something different, in both languages: it sets one of the function's inputs. In `mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)`, `na.rm = TRUE` does not create an object called `na.rm`. It tells `mean()` to leave out missing values (slide "Functions and their inputs").

:::

## Values and their types

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The types

Every value has a **type**. The type decides what can be done with it.

| Type | Examples | What it is | Python's name |
|---|---|---|---|
| numeric | `1`, `1.3`, `-999` | A number, whole or with decimals | `int` (whole), `float` (decimals) |
| character | `"Nebraska"`, `"31001"` | Text, always written inside quotation marks | `str` |
| logical | `TRUE`, `FALSE` | The answer to a yes-or-no question | `bool`, written `True`, `False` |

In R you will also see **integer** (a whole number written with an `L`, such as `3L`); it behaves like numeric.

Quotation marks matter: `"31001"` is text, `31001` is a number. You cannot do arithmetic on text:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: text-arithmetic
"5" + 1
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
"5" + 1
```
:::
::::

### Operators

Arithmetic and comparisons follow the usual signs, with a few that may be new:

| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+ - * /` | add, subtract, multiply, divide | `6 / 4` | `r 6 / 4` |
| `^` (R), `**` (Python) | to the power of | `2^3`, `2 ** 3` | `r 2^3` |
| `==`, `!=` | is equal to, is not equal to | `5 == 4` | `r 5 == 4` |
| `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` | greater than, less than, and so on | `5 > 4` | `r 5 > 4` |

In Python, `^` is not a power: it means something else and gives a wrong number without an error. A comparison gives back a logical value. `==` (two equals signs) asks a question; a single `=` sets a value. Comparisons are how rows are kept or dropped from a table later in the course.

### Missing values: `NA`

`NA` means "this value is missing". It is not zero, and it is not the text `"NA"`. In Python's table package, pandas, a missing number is printed `NaN` ("not a number"), and plain Python uses `None`.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: na
yields
is.na(yields)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yields = pd.Series([150, 162, None, 171])
yields.isna()
```
:::
::::

`is.na()` and `.isna()` ask of each value "is it missing?". The third one is.

In R, most calculations that include a missing value give `NA`, because the true answer is unknown: `mean(yields)` gives `NA`. pandas does the opposite. Both are on the slide "Functions and their inputs", tab "Defaults".

:::

## Vectors and tables

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Vectors

A **vector** is a sequence of values, all of the **same type**. In R, `c()` (short for "combine") makes one. In Python, AI-written code uses an **array** from the numpy package, `np.array([...])`, for the same job.

Arithmetic on vectors works **element by element**: the first value with the first, the second with the second, and so on.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: vector-arithmetic
v <- c(4, 3, 5, 9, 1)
v * 2
v + c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import numpy as np
v = np.array([4, 3, 5, 9, 1])
print(v * 2)
print(v + np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]))
```
:::
::::

Code rarely needs a loop to do the same thing to every value; this is why. A plain Python list, `[4, 3, 5, 9, 1]` without `np.array`, is different: `* 2` repeats the list instead of doubling each value.

### One type per vector

A vector can hold only one type. Mix types, and everything is converted to the type that can hold all of them, **without an error**:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: mixed
mixed <- c(4, 3, "5", 9, 1)
mixed
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import numpy as np
mixed = np.array([4, 3, "5", 9, 1])
mixed
```
:::
::::

Every value is now text (note the quotation marks; numpy adds `dtype='<U21'`, its name for text). One text value turned the whole vector into text. When a column of numbers arrives in your analysis as text, this is usually why, and arithmetic on it will then fail or give `NA`.

### Tables

A **table** holds data in rows and columns. Each column is a vector, so each column has one type, but different columns can have different types. All columns have the same length. R and pandas both call a table a **data frame**; this course says table.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: table
yield_data <- data.frame(
  nitrogen = c(200, 180, 300),
  yield = c(240, 220, 230),
  state = c("Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa")
)
yield_data
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yield_data = pd.DataFrame({
  "nitrogen": [200, 180, 300],
  "yield": [240, 220, 230],
  "state": ["Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa"]
})
yield_data
```
:::
::::

Each `name = c(...)` in R, or `"name": [...]` in Python, makes one column. Values in the same position make one row. pandas also prints the row numbers, counting from 0.

You will also see **tibble** and **data.table**. They are tables too, with some extra conveniences; read them as tables.

### Other objects you will see

+ **list**: holds any mix of objects, each of any type and length. Results of a statistical model usually come back as a list. Python's version with names is a **dictionary**, written `{"name": value, ...}`.
+ **matrix**: values of one type in rows and columns, used for linear algebra. You will rarely meet one in this course.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: list
a_list <- list(numbers = c(10, 20), state = "Iowa")
names(a_list)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
a_dict = {"numbers": [10, 20], "state": "Iowa"}
a_dict.keys()
```
:::
::::

`names()` and `.keys()` both give the names of the parts.

### What kind of object is it?

Many surprises come from an object not being what you thought: a column of text instead of numbers, a vector instead of a table. A few functions tell you:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: class-str
class(yield_data)
str(yield_data)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yield_data = pd.DataFrame({
  "nitrogen": [200, 180, 300],
  "state": ["Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa"]
})
print(type(yield_data))
print(yield_data.dtypes)
```
:::
::::

`class()` and `type()` give the kind of object. `str()` gives the size and the type of every column (`num` numeric, `chr` character); pandas' `.dtypes` gives the type of every column, with `object` for text.

:::

## Pulling parts out of an object

AI-written code constantly takes one column, some rows or one value out of an object. Whatever the object, it is done with brackets, in one of a few patterns.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

| Pattern | Gives | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vector[position]` | values at those positions | `v[2]` | `r v[2]` |
| `table$column` | one column, as a vector | `yield_data$yield` | `r out(yield_data$yield)` |
| `table[condition, ]` | the rows where the condition is `TRUE`; the empty place after the comma means "all columns" | `yield_data[yield_data$yield > 225, ]` | the `r sum(yield_data$yield > 225)` rows with `yield` above 225 |
| `list[[position]]` or `list$name` | one element of a list | `a_list$state` | `r a_list$state` |

Positions count from 1. `table$column` is the one you will see most often: `mean(yield_data$yield)` reads "the average of the `yield` column of `yield_data`". The condition is itself a comparison that gives one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per row, and the rows marked `TRUE` are kept:

```{webr-r}
#| label: extract
#| code-track: 0.5
yield_data$yield > 225
yield_data[yield_data$yield > 225, ]
```

### Python

| Pattern | Gives | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `array[position]` | the value at that position | `v[1]` | `r v[2]` |
| `table["column"]` | one column | `yield_data["yield"]` | `r out(yield_data$yield)` |
| `table[condition]` | the rows where the condition is `True` | `yield_data[yield_data["yield"] > 225]` | the `r sum(yield_data$yield > 225)` rows with `yield` above 225 |
| `dictionary["name"]` | one element of a dictionary | `a_dict["state"]` | `r a_list$state` |

**Positions count from 0 in Python**, so `v[1]` is the second value, the one R calls `v[2]`. Code that mixes the two up runs without an error and takes the wrong value.

```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yield_data = pd.DataFrame({"yield": [240, 220, 230], "state": ["Kansas", "Nebraska", "Iowa"]})
print(yield_data["yield"].mean())
print(yield_data[yield_data["yield"] > 225])
```

:::

## Functions and their inputs

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The pattern

A **function** takes inputs, does something with them, and gives back a result. Every function call follows the same pattern, in R and in Python (with `=` in place of `<-`):

```{r}
#| eval: false
result <- function_name(first_input, name = value, ...)
```

| Part | What it is | Required? |
|---|---|---|
| `result <-` | Stores what the function gives back | No; without it, the result is printed and then gone |
| `function_name` | What to do | Yes |
| `( )` | Holds the inputs, separated by commas. R and Python call the inputs **arguments** | Yes, even if empty |
| `first_input` | Usually the data to work on, matched by its **position** | Usually |
| `name = value` | An option, matched by its **name** | No; each has a default |

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: round
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
round(3.14159, ndigits=2)
```
:::
::::

In this real call, the first input, `3.14159`, is the number to round. `digits = 2` (`ndigits=2` in Python) is an option. Leave it out and `round()` uses its default, 0 digits: `round(3.14159)` gives `r round(3.14159)`.

### Functions you will see

All of these follow the pattern. You do not need to remember them; you need to recognise the pattern when you see them.

| Function | What it gives back | Example | Result | In Python |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mean()`, `sum()`, `min()`, `max()` | one number summarising a vector | `sum(v)` | `r sum(v)` | `v.mean()`, `sum()`, `min()`, `max()` |
| `length()` | how many values a vector has | `length(v)` | `r length(v)` | `len()` |
| `nrow()`, `ncol()` | rows or columns of a table | `nrow(yield_data)` | `r nrow(yield_data)` | `len(table)`, `table.shape` |
| `round()` | rounded numbers | `round(2.567, digits = 1)` | `r round(2.567, digits = 1)` | `round()` |
| `seq()` | a sequence of numbers | `seq(0, 10, by = 5)` | `r out(seq(0, 10, by = 5))` | `range()`, `np.arange()` |
| `rep()` | repeated values | `rep(10, times = 3)` | `r out(rep(10, times = 3))` | `np.repeat()` |
| `is.na()` | `TRUE` where a value is missing | `is.na(c(1, NA))` | `r out(is.na(c(1, NA)))` | `.isna()` |
| `class()`, `str()` | what kind of object something is | `class(v)` | `r class(v)` | `type()`, `.dtypes` |

### Defaults

Every option has a **default**: the value it takes when you do not set it, chosen by whoever wrote the function. R's `mean()` has an option `na.rm` (remove `NA`s) whose default is `FALSE`, so the average of `yields` comes back `NA`. pandas' `.mean()` has the opposite default: its option `skipna` is `True`, so it leaves missing values out unless told not to.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: na-rm
mean(yields)
mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yields = pd.Series([150, 162, None, 171])
print(yields.mean())
print(yields.mean(skipna=False))
```
:::
::::

Leaving out the missing value, the average is of the `r sum(!is.na(yields))` values that are there: (150 + 162 + 171) / 3 = `r mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)`.

:::{.callout-important}
AI-written R code often adds `na.rm = TRUE` as a matter of routine, and pandas does it unasked. Either way, missing values are removed **without saying how many**. An average of 3 values out of 4 is fine; an average of 3 out of 300 is not. When you see `na.rm = TRUE`, or an average computed in pandas, ask how many values were left out.
:::

### Variations you will see

AI-written code often arranges the same pattern differently. These change how the code looks, not what it does:

+ **One call inside another**: `round(mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 1)`. Read from the inside out: first the average, then round it.
+ **Spread over several lines**: a long call, like `data.frame(...)` above, is split after commas. It is still one call; the closing `)` ends it.
+ **Inputs without names**: `round(3.14159, 2)` is the same as `round(3.14159, digits = 2)`, because `digits` is the second input. Named inputs are easier to read; Python calls them **keyword arguments**.
+ **The pipe** (R), `|>`: `yields |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)` means `mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)`. The object on the left becomes the first input of the function on the right. You will see it in nearly every chapter from Chapter 3 on.
+ **Functions after a dot** (Python): `yields.mean()` is the function `mean` applied to `yields`. Python code is full of these, and they are chained left to right, as the pipe is: `yields.dropna().mean()` drops the missing values, then averages.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: pipe
yields |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
yields = pd.Series([150, 162, None, 171])
yields.dropna().mean()
```
:::
::::

:::

## Reading a help page

Every function has a help page. Put `?` in front of its name, as in `?seq`, and R opens the page; in Python, `help(round)` prints the one for `round`. The R inside these slides cannot show help pages, so this slide shows the parts of the `?seq` page that matter. Three sections tell you most of what you need.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Description

At the top, one or two sentences on what the function does. For `seq()`: "Generate regular sequences." If that is not what you wanted, you are on the wrong page.

### Usage

The function's inputs, in order, each with its default. The real `?seq` page also covers some related functions (`seq_len()`, `seq_along()` and others), so its Usage section lists several lines. The one for `seq()` itself is under `## Default S3 method:`, a technical label you can ignore:

```r
seq(from = 1, to = 1, by = ((to - from)/(length.out - 1)),
    length.out = NULL, along.with = NULL, ...)
```

+ Each `name = value` is an input and its default. Leave out `from`, and it is 1.
+ Inputs without names are matched by position: `seq(0, 10)` means `from = 0, to = 10`.
+ `NULL` means "not set". `...` means further inputs can be passed on; you can ignore it.

You only supply the inputs whose defaults you want to change. That is why `seq(0, 10)` works although `seq()` lists five inputs.

### Arguments, Examples, or ask

**Arguments** says what each input means. For `seq()`, `by` is the step between values and `length.out` is how many values you want, so the same sequence can be described two ways:

```{webr-r}
#| label: seq-two-ways
seq(0, 1, by = 0.25)
seq(0, 1, length.out = 5)
```

**Examples**, at the very bottom, is code you can copy and run. Running an example and then looking back at Usage is often the fastest way to understand a function.

You can also paste a line into an AI assistant and ask what each input does (see the slide "Requests you can copy", tab "Explain code"). The help page is the reference to check its answer against: it describes the version of the function installed on your computer, which the AI cannot see.

:::

## Packages

::: {.panel-tabset}

### What are packages?

A package is a drawer in your workspace (the R environment) holding specialized tools (functions) for a particular set of tasks. Packages are written by R's users and shared for free; most of the functions in this course come from them.

**Example packages:**

+ dplyr (data wrangling)
+ data.table (data wrangling)
+ ggplot2 (data visualization)
+ sf (spatial vector data handling)
+ terra (spatial raster data handling)
+ stars (spatiotemporal data handling)

**tidyverse** is a package that installs and loads a set of others at once, including dplyr, ggplot2 and readr.

Python has packages too. The ones in this lecture are **pandas** (tables), **numpy** (arrays of numbers) and **matplotlib** (figures).

### What you will see

Two kinds of line about packages appear in AI-written code and AI messages:

+ `library(ggplot2)` in R, `import pandas as pd` in Python, at the top of a document: the code **loads** the package, so that its functions can be used further down. `as pd` gives pandas the short name `pd`, which the code then writes in front of its functions. A document loads its packages every time it runs.
+ `install.packages("ggplot2")` in R, `pip install pandas` for Python: the AI **installs** the package, that is, downloads it onto your computer. This is a one-time step that sets up the computer, which the AI runs for you. It should never be inside a document.

### Which package is a function from?

`dplyr::filter()` reads "the function `filter` from the package `dplyr`". In Python, `pd.read_csv()` reads "the function `read_csv` from the package imported as `pd`", that is, pandas, and `pd.DataFrame()` below is pandas' function that makes a table.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
dplyr::filter(yield_data, yield > 225)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame({"yield": [240, 230]})
```
:::
::::

:::

# When code fails

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Errors, and failures without one

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Reading an error

When R or Python cannot run a line, it stops and prints an error. Read it before anything else: it usually names the function that failed and what it objected to.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: error-sum
sum("a")
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
sum(["a"])
```
:::
::::

R's "invalid 'type' (character) of argument" and Python's "unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'" say the same thing: `sum()` ran, but its input was text, and text cannot be added up. Python's first word, `TypeError`, names the kind of error.

### Errors you will see

Two errors you will see often:

| R says | Python says | What it means | Usual cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| `object 'x' not found` | `NameError: name 'x' is not defined` | No object has that name | A typo (`Yield` and `yield` are different names), or the line that creates it was never run, or it was made in the Console but not in the document |
| `non-numeric argument to binary operator` | `TypeError: ... 'str' and 'int'` | Arithmetic on something that is not a number | A number stored as text |

When you ask an AI about an error, send the **whole** error message, the code that produced it, and what you expected. The AI cannot see your screen.

### No error is not the same as right

An error is the good case: you know something went wrong. Worse are lines that run and give a wrong answer. Two you have already met:

+ One text value in `c(...)` or `np.array([...])` turned every value to text, with no error.
+ `na.rm = TRUE`, and pandas by default, leave out missing values without saying how many.

And one more. Text that looks like numbers is sorted as text, character by character:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{webr-r}
#| label: sort-text
sort(c("9", "10", "100"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{pyodide-python}
sorted(["9", "10", "100"])
```
:::
::::

"10" comes before "9" because "1" comes before "9". No error, wrong order. Checking the type of a value (`class()`, `str()`, `type()`, `.dtypes`) would catch it.

:::{.callout-important}
Code that runs is not the same as code that is right. Deciding whether it is right is the part that stays your job.
:::

:::

# Asking AI

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## What the AI cannot know

The AI knows R and Python. It does not know your session or your intentions. Each of these has to be in your request:

1. **The code**: paste the exact lines, not a description of them
2. **What came out**: the whole error message or output, copied, not retyped from memory
3. **What you expected**: the result you thought you would get, and why
4. **What is around it**: which objects already exist and what they hold, which packages you loaded. Running `str()` on an object and pasting the output is a quick way to describe it
5. **What you want back**: an explanation, a corrected line, or both

:::{.callout-tip title="Using an agent in your editor or terminal?"}
An agent such as Claude Code can run the code and see the error itself. Still say what you expected **before** it runs, so you have something to compare its answer with.
:::

## A weak request and a strong one

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Weak

```text
My R code doesn't work, please fix it.
```

The AI does not see the code, the error or what you wanted. It will guess, and a typical reply is a list of five common R mistakes, none of which may be yours.

### Strong

```text
I ran these two lines:

yields <- c(150, 162, NA, 171)
average_yield <- mean(yields)

average_yield prints NA. I expected the average of the three yields
that are not missing, 161. Explain in one plain-English sentence why I
got NA, then correct the code. Also print how many values the average
used.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/yields.qmd, under the
heading "Average yield", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

The last paragraph is the **closing instructions**: the same lines end every request that asks for code. They make the AI put its code into a Quarto document, with a sentence above each piece of code, so that the result is a web page you can read and keep. Chapter 2 teaches Quarto; the full text is on the slide "Requests you can copy".

`here::here()` builds a file's path from the top folder of your project, so the path works on any computer. Chapter 3 explains it.

### What came back

What the AI's answer looks like in the rendered page: a sentence, then the code it describes. Read each sentence, and check that the code under it does what the sentence says.

`mean()` gives `NA` when any value is missing, unless told to leave missing values out with `na.rm = TRUE`.

```{webr-r}
#| label: ai-answer-mean
average_yield <- mean(yields, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Print the checks: how many values there are, how many are missing, and the average of the rest.

```{webr-r}
#| label: ai-answer-check
cat(
  paste("values: expected 4, got", length(yields)),
  paste("missing values: expected 1, got", sum(is.na(yields))),
  paste("values used: expected 3, got", sum(!is.na(yields))),
  paste("average yield: expected 161, got", average_yield),
  sep = "\n"
)
```

Every check matches, and each line says what it is checking. Two functions that may be new: `cat()` prints text, and `paste()` joins pieces of text into one. `sum(!is.na(yields))` counts the values that are **not** missing (`!` means "not").

:::

## Requests you can copy

Copy one, then replace every `<...>` with what **you** know. The blanks are the part the AI cannot fill in for you. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Closing instructions

The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave "expected X, got Y" as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:

```text
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your `.qmd` and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.

### Explain code

For code you did not write, or code you are not sure about:

```text
Explain this R code to me. For each line, write one plain-English
sentence. Then list:
1. any line that would only work on the computer it was written on
2. any line that could give a wrong result without an error, and what
   check would reveal it

<paste the code here>
```

### Explain an error

```text
I ran this R code:

<paste the code here>

and got this message:

<paste the whole error or warning here>

I expected <what you expected to get>. The objects it uses hold
<what they hold, or the output of str() on each>, and I loaded the
packages <package names>. Explain in plain English what the message
means and which line caused it, then correct the code.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

:::

# Checking the result

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Checking: what to ask for, and why

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Checks you can know in advance

A check is only useful if you know the right answer before you see the result. The AI can write the checking code; only you can supply the answer. Sources of answers you know in advance:

| | Ask the AI to print | You know the answer from |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | how many values, rows or columns there are | counting, or the description of the data (a help page, a codebook) |
| 2 | the type of each key value or column | knowing what it measures: a yield is a number, a state name is text |
| 3 | how many values are missing | the data's description, or counting them yourself on a small case |
| 4 | the smallest and largest value | what is believable: a corn yield is not negative |
| 5 | the result on a small case | working it out by hand, as for the average of 150, 162 and 171 |

### Asking for them

Say what you expect, and ask for each check in one form, so the rendered page says which passed:

```text
I expect <number> values, <number> of them missing, and an average of
<number>. Print each check on its own line as "name of check: expected
X, got Y".
```

If you cannot fill in a blank, that is a sign to look at the data, or its description, before asking.

### A check that fails

A student expected the values to be numbers. The AI's code, and what it printed:

```{webr-r}
#| label: chk-fail
cat("type of mixed: expected numeric, got", class(mixed), "\n")
```

The check fails: `mixed` holds text. Nothing errored, and any average of it would be wrong or `NA`. The right move is to find out where the text came from (here, the `"5"` written in quotation marks) before going on.

:::

## Your turn: read the AI's code

A student asked an AI to "average my yields", and got this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(dplyr)
my_yields <- c(150, 162, "171", 140)
avg = mean(my_yields)
avg
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Questions

A. What does each of the four lines do?

B. What will `avg` print, and why? Is there an error?

C. Which check from the previous slide would have caught the problem, and what would it have printed?

D. Is line 1 needed?

### Answers

```{r}
#| label: your-turn
#| include: false
my_yields <- c(150, 162, "171", 140)
avg <- suppressWarnings(mean(my_yields))
```

A. Loads the dplyr package; stores four yields under the name `my_yields`; computes their average and stores it as `avg` (`=` does the same as `<-` here); prints `avg`.

B. `r avg`. Because `"171"` is in quotation marks, the whole vector is text, and the average of text is `NA`. There is no error, only a warning ("argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA"), which is easy to miss.

C. Check 2, the type: "type of my_yields: expected numeric, got `r class(my_yields)`".

D. No. None of the functions used (`c()`, `mean()`) comes from dplyr; both are built into R. It does no harm, but a line you cannot explain is worth asking about.

To see B for yourself, run the student's code:

```{webr-r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
my_yields <- c(150, 162, "171", 140)
avg = mean(my_yields)
avg
```

:::

# Summary

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## What you must understand, and what the AI can write

| You need to understand | The AI can write |
|---|---|
| What an object is, and that `<-` (`=` in Python) stores a result under a name, replacing any old one | The names and the assignments |
| That `table$column` (`table["column"]` in Python) takes one column out of a table | The extraction code |
| The types of values, and that mixing them converts everything to text without an error | The conversions between types |
| The pattern of a function call: name, inputs by position, options by name, defaults | Which function to use and which options to set |
| What a default does, especially `na.rm = TRUE` | The options themselves |
| That a help page lists each input and its default | Which inputs to set |
| That `library()` or `import` at the top of a document loads a package, and that installing is a one-time setup of the computer that never goes in a document | The `library()` and `import` lines, and installing the packages |
| How Python differs: `=`, positions from 0, `**`, functions after a dot | Code in either language |
| What the two common errors mean | The fix, once you have told it the code, the error and what you expected |
| What a correct result looks like | The checking code |

**Every time AI hands you code:** read it line by line, and name the objects, functions, inputs and packages in it. If you cannot say what a line does, ask before you keep it. Then judge the result by checks whose answer you knew beforehand.
